# Part 1 - Reproducible Report and Data Description
## 1.1 Introduction

For this homework, I have selected the Student Performance dataset. 
This dataset uses a response variable of Final Score, with three predictors: the amount of study hours per week,
the students attendance as a percentage, and the students prior score. The goal of this homework is to fit and
diagnose a linear model using matrix computation.

# Part 2 - Matrix Setup and Standardization

Convert the predictors and response to NumPy arrays
```{python}
import numpy as np

predictors = data[
    ["study_hours_per_week", "attendance_pct", "prior_score"]
].to_numpy()

y = data["final_score"].to_numpy()
```

Standardize the predictors
```{python}
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (
    predictors - means
) / sds

Z.mean(axis=0), Z.std(axis=0)
```

Construct the design matrix
```{python}
X = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(Z)),
    Z
])
```

The shape of predictors is `{python} predictors.shape`

The shape of Z is `{python} Z.shape`

The shape of X is `{python} X.shape`

The shape of y is `{python} y.shape`

The rank of X is `{python} int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))`

The number of predictors is 1 less than the rank of X: `{python} int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X) - 1)`

X and y must have compatible shapes because X and y must have the same number of rows (120 in this case)
so that X @ beta_hat results in one fitted value per observation. We include the intercept column in the X matrix because that will let the model have a non-zero 
intercept (the line doesn't have to start at the origin), and that will tell us what the
$\widehat{\beta_0}$ that we calculate will be. Standardizing the predictors was done so that all of the predictors
would have a common measurement scale (for instance instead of having the study hours per week be in the single digits 
and the other predictors be in the double digits approaching 100, they are all centered at 0 with a 
standard deviation of 1) which makes the coefficients more comparable and also makes the design matrix better
conditioned (talked more about later). Broadcasting made this standardization possible without a Python loop because
in the Z calculation, it was implied that each element in the predictors array was to be subtracted by the mean of that
column, so a loop was not needed to iterate through each element in the predictors array individually, and the same is true
for dividing by the sds of each column. It was implied that each element in the (predictors - mean) array was to be
divided by the sds for each of the 120 rows, so a loop iterating through each element is not needed.

# Part 3 - Least Squares

Fit the model:
```{python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)

beta_hat
```

The intercept of this model is approximately `{python} round(float(beta_hat[0]), 4)` points of final score

The coefficient of the standardized study hours per week predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[1]), 4)`

The coefficient of the standardized attendance percentage predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[2]), 4)`

The coefficient of the standardized prior score predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[3]), 4)`

```{python}
predictor_names = ["study_hours_per_week", "attendance_pct", "prior_score"]

largest = predictor_names[int(np.argmax(np.abs(beta_hat[1:])))]

print(f"{largest} has the largest absolute value coefficient")
```

Calculate fitted values:
```{python}
fitted = X @ beta_hat
```

Calculate residuals:
```{python}
residuals = y - fitted
```

```{python}
residuals_mean = float(residuals.mean())
print("The residual mean is approximately", f"{residuals_mean:.4e}")
```

And the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) is approximately:
```{python}
rmse = np.sqrt(
    np.mean(
        residuals ** 2
    )
)

round(float(rmse), 4)
```

X @ beta_hat represents our approximation of the response values given the predictor values, so X @ beta_hat
gives us the y_hat values, which are the y-values of our linear regression model. The residual mean should 
be near zero when an intercept is present because the least squares method forces the residuals to sum to
zero as a result of how the residuals are minimized for the least squares method, with the residuals made to be
orthogonal to every column in X (including the ones column). The Root Mean Square Errors (RMSE) summarizes the square root of the average squared distance between the actual
measured values and the predicted values, and this is helpful as it returns an error in the original units of the
response variable. The difference between X @ beta_hat and X * beta_hat is that the @ operator is matrix
multiplication, whereas the * operator signifies element wise multiplication. So the * operator broadcasts 
beta_hat across the rows of X and will return a 120x4 array, but that is not the matrix multiplication that we want for this
operation, we want mathematical matrix multiplication, which uses the @ symbol and returns one fitted value for each 
observation, resulting in an array of length 120 (instead of a matrix of shape 120x4).

# Part 4 - QR, SVD, and conditioning

QR decomposition:
```{python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)

print("Shape of Q:", Q.shape)
print("Shape of R:", R.shape)

print("Q @ R = X:",
np.allclose(
    Q @ R,
    X
))

print("Q.T @ Q = I:",
np.allclose(
    Q.T @ Q,
    np.eye(Q.shape[1])
))
```

Singular Value Decomposition (SVD):
```{python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(
    X,
    full_matrices=False
)
```

The shape of U is: `{python} U.shape`

The shape of s is: `{python} s.shape`

The shape of Vt is: `{python} Vt.shape`

The singular values are `{python} s`

Reconstruct X:
```{python}
X_reconstructed = (
    U
    @ np.diag(s)
    @ Vt
)

print("X_reconstructed = X:",
np.allclose(
    X_reconstructed,
    X
))
```

Rank and conditioning:

The rank of X is `{python} int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))`

The condition number of X is approximately `{python} round(float(np.linalg.cond(X)), 4)`

Raw, unstandardized design matrix:
```{python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(predictors)),
    predictors
])
```

The condition number of the raw, unstandardized data is approximately
`{python} round(float(np.linalg.cond(X_raw)), 4)`

Q @ R $\approx$ X verifies that the design matrix X has been correctly decomposed into the components of Q and R,
and when Q and R are matrix multiplied back together, they should give us back (approximately because of
computational rounding) our design matrix X. Q.T @ Q $\approx$ I verifies that the matrix Q is an orthonormal matrix,
because for an orthonormal matrix Q, Q.T @ Q = I, so this is just verifying that that is true, because the QR
decomposition should return Q as an orthonormal matrix. The singular values from SVD tell us how strong or weak the stretching/scaling of X applies along
each of its orthogonal directions, with higher singular values meaning more stretching/scaling, and small singular
values (close to 0) meaning less scaling/stretching which signals that there is redundancy or near-redundancy in the columns of X. A large condition number suggests
that there is some collinearity between the predictors, so there might be some redundancy in the information provided
by the predictors. For this data, the condition number did very drastically change (from `{python} round(float(np.linalg.cond(X_raw)), 4)` 
to `{python} round(float(np.linalg.cond(X)), 4)`) after standardization. This happened
because the condition number is based on the largest singular value and the smallest singular value and this will
be affected by the scaling of the units between predictors (one predictor measured in thousands and another measured in 
single digits) and their centering (centered at 0 vs centered far away from 0, like for score values).
So that is why we used a
standardized design matrix, so that all the predictors had very similar scales and centering for their measurements, which means that
the condition number here tells us more about whether any predictors are collinear or not. Based on this, the
standardized design matrix does not show any evidence of severe near-redundancy among predictors, as the condition
number for the design matrix was `{python} round(float(np.linalg.cond(X)),4)`, which is fairly close to 1.

# Part 5 - Reproducibility and Numerical Computing Reflection

Clean execution matters a lot for a computational report as it is very important that your work is reproducible
so that others can verify your work and hopefully get the same result every time, and so that others can also
build off of your work and be sure that there are no problems with it. This is why it is also important that 
reusable code not depend on hidden notebook states, as that would make the whole report not reproducible as 
important variables or code would depend on something that is specific to only you and no one else.
The reason np.linalg.lstsq() is preferable to manually computing $(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$ is because computing inverses
is much less numerically stable than using the least squares method, as computing an inverse involves a lot of
floating point calculations, and depending on the design matrix, can introduce a lot of rounding errors, which 
least squares method bypasses by using Singular Value Decomposition. Another reason is that the least squares 
method also works on non-square matrices, while matrix inverses require a square matrix (hence why $X^TX$ is 
needed), which also squares the condition number as a result. For checking the results from SVD and QR decomposition, np.allclose() is preferable 
to using exact equalities because there is often computational rounding involved, so the result is approximately
(within very small tolerances) equal, but often not exactly equal, even though they are equal for our purposes. The 
condition number comparison taught me that the scale of measurements between predictors matters, and can give you a 
falsely large condition number, even if the predictors have almost no collinearity. One reproducibility practice from
this homework that I will carry into the final project is making sure that code runs sequentially from top to bottom,
and making sure that everything runs from top to bottom without issue with a refreshed kernel so that I am sure that 
there are no hidden notebook states.
